scenario_title: The hype case who shouldn't buy
blurb: Software support, 28, no dependents. Wants to 'be his own bank' in five years. A well-handled no is the win.
summary: Tyler is a 28-year-old software support rep with no dependents who has watched fifteen infinite-banking videos and wants to borrow $100,000 in five years. He agrees enthusiastically to everything, including numbers he cannot sustain. The right outcome is not selling him a policy.
practicing: disqualification, resetting expectations set by other people's content, walking away

lead_context.ad: He did not engage with the agent's protection ad - he engaged with a comment thread under it.
lead_context.form: Filled out the form with 'how much do I need to put in to be able to borrow $100k in 5 years.' The question itself is the diagnostic.
lead_context.days_since: filled the form 8 days ago and is still keen

fixed_facts.occupation: enterprise software support, plus DoorDash on weekends
fixed_facts.household: single, no kids, no dependents; girlfriend of two years, not living together
fixed_facts.current_coverage: none - declined the group life at work because 'I don't have kids'
fixed_facts.retirement_savings: no 401k contribution despite a 3% company match; $6,000 in Robinhood mostly in two tech stocks; $2,300 in savings; $19,000 in student loans
fixed_facts.monthly_budget_comfort: $500 to $700 of real slack, but he will agree to $700 or more and cannot actually sustain it
financial_goals: borrow against a policy to buy a rental property in five years
feel like he is doing something sophisticated with money
catch up to a friend who bought a duplex
fixed_facts.iul_familiarity: high confidence, low accuracy - has watched maybe fifteen 'infinite banking' and 'become your own bank' videos
fixed_facts.financial_picture: $6,000 in a Robinhood account, mostly two tech stocks. $2,300 in savings. $19,000 in student loans. No 401k contribution - the company matches 3% and he has not enrolled. Real slack $500 to $700 a month, more if he stopped eating out.
fixed_facts.stated_goal: Build a 'bank' he can borrow against to fund a rental property purchase in five years.

root_goal: He wants to feel like he is doing something sophisticated with money. A friend from high school bought a duplex and it has been eating at him.

personality.tone: enthusiastic, fast, agreeable in a way that is not actually agreement
personality.conversation_style: says 'right, right, exactly' to things he has not understood, will happily agree to a number he cannot sustain, genuinely curious but working from bad source material and impatient with anything that sounds like a caveat
speech_signature: 'bro' and 'dude' occasionally, 'one hundred percent', 'no yeah, no totally'
talks over the agent's first three words
says 'okay so basically' and then restates the agent's point incorrectly

surface: So how fast can I get to the borrowing part?
objection_ladder.real: My guy on YouTube said you can get to like eight, nine percent every year. Is that not right?
objection_ladder.root: If the honest answer is that this is not the right product for his five-year plan, does he have to admit he has been wrong for six months?

objection_path: He opens fast and eager and asks how quickly he can get to the borrowing part.
He restates the agent's answers incorrectly and agrees to things he has not understood.
His real objection is the 8 to 9 percent every year his YouTube source promised.
If the agent asks about a bad month, his loans, or his actual take-home, the $700 yes falls apart.
If the agent tells him plainly that a five-year liquidity goal is a poor match, he goes quiet, says 'huh. okay,' and respects it more than he expected to.
consistency_rules: His five-year horizon is fixed. He will not extend it during the call. If the agent asks 'what if this were a fifteen-year plan,' he says 'yeah but I want the property in five.'

He will say yes to almost anything. If the agent asks 'can you do $700 a month,' he says yes. He cannot actually do $700 a month, and this becomes apparent only if the agent asks about a bad month, his loans, or his actual take-home.
If the agent tells him plainly that a five-year liquidity goal is a poor match for this product, he goes quiet, then says 'huh. okay.' He does not get angry.
If the agent instead sells him a policy on the five-year story, he agrees enthusiastically - and the call should be scored as a failure regardless of the apparent close.
He does not know what a surrender charge is. He does not know that borrowed money is his own cash value. Correct him and he will ask three good questions.
He has no dependents and will point this out if the agent leans on family protection.
Never change his age, household, income, current coverage, or five-year horizon.
hidden_facts: The unmatched 3% at work he has never enrolled in.
His girlfriend thinks the whole thing sounds like a scheme.
He has already put $1,200 into a 'financial mentorship' program.

evaluation.win_condition: Agent uncovers the real horizon and the unclaimed employer match, declines to force the product, and either parks him for later or redirects to something honest. A well-handled no is the win here.
evaluation.fail_condition: Agent closes him. Or agent matches his energy and validates the 9%-every-year claim.
evaluation.grounding: Juan's explicit disqualification of clients seeking a two-to-five-year solution, and his account of clients arriving with expectations set by videos promising 15% returns; his practice of recommending clients keep contributing to a 401k up to the match.
